FIFO.title: FIFO — First In, First Out
FIFO.subtitle: First-Come, First-Served Scheduling
FIFO.description: In the FIFO algorithm, tasks are executed on free cores in the exact order they arrive in the ready queue. This is one of the simplest scheduling algorithms taught in OS reference books (e.g., Silberschatz & Tanenbaum) as an introductory concept.
keyPoints: This algorithm is Non-preemptive; no running task can be interrupted by another task.
It is fair in terms of arrival order, but can suffer from the 'Convoy Effect' where short tasks wait behind long ones.
In this simulator, when a core becomes idle, the first task in queue is assigned regardless of priority.

PRIORITY.title: Priority Scheduling
PRIORITY.subtitle: Scheduling based on task importance
PRIORITY.description: In Priority Scheduling, each task has a priority value. The scheduler always picks the highest priority task available. If a higher priority task arrives while all cores are busy, the lowest priority running task is preempted.
keyPoints: This version is Preemptive; a running task can be interrupted by a higher priority arrival.
Context Switching state saving is intentionally omitted for preemption here, causing preempted tasks to restart from 0% progress upon returning to the queue.
This reflects a system without process control blocks (PCB) context saving for educational demonstration of preemptive vs non-preemptive concepts.
Can lead to Starvation: low-priority tasks may never complete if high-priority tasks arrive continuously.
PRIORITY.note: Note: On multi-core systems, if an idle core is available when a high-priority task arrives, the dispatcher assigns it directly without preemption. Preempted tasks re-entering queue may execute simultaneously on other free cores.

ROUND_ROBIN.title: Round Robin
ROUND_ROBIN.subtitle: Fair scheduling based on time quantum
ROUND_ROBIN.description: In Round Robin, each task gets a fixed time slice (Time Quantum). If unfinished within this time, it is preempted, state is saved, and moved to the back of the queue. This is the foundation of modern time-sharing operating systems.
keyPoints: Unlike Priority, preemption occurs purely due to time expiration (Time Quantum).
Context Saving is implemented in this simulator; preempted tasks resume exact progress when scheduled again.
Tasks preempted by time quantum return to the end of the ready queue to maintain round-robin fairness.
Selecting Time Quantum size is crucial: too small increases context switch overhead, too large degrades to FIFO.
ROUND_ROBIN.note: Note: Context switching overhead is simulated without time penalty here for clarity.
